text: Learning which objects may safely contact each other.
Handle electrostatic-sensitive components (e.g., holding a motherboard by the edges without touching pins).
Perform tight-space cable management (routing, zipping, and hiding cables behind a desk or PC chassis).
Dust computer internals using compressed air while holding fans stationary to prevent over-spinning.
Plug cables into rear I/O ports by feel or from tight visual angles (e.g., distinguishing DisplayPort from HDMI by touch/shape).
Sharpen knives using a whetstone or pull-through sharpener.
Operate high-risk manual kitchen tools (e.g., mandoline slicer, box grater) without damaging the tool or the robot's end-effectors.

Wake someone up; help someone sit, stand, or steady themselves; offer an arm on stairs; help with buttons, zips, and shoes; fetch and clean glasses and hearing aids; push or fold a wheelchair or walker.
Hospitality: simple cocktails and mocktails, uncork wine, open cans and bottles, offer slippers, follow household rules on who may be served alcohol.

Primitives: communication is thin (you have Report, Alert, and Ask for clarification). Add Speak, Listen, Announce, Explain, Confirm, Refuse, Undo, Hand off to a human, Remember, Forget. Physical verbs also missing: Cut/Slice, Peel, Crack, Tear, Hammer, Drill, Climb, Kneel/Crouch, Balance, Throw/Catch, Point/Gesture, Spray, Brush.

intentionally left out, and where everything belongs.
“Make this place look nice.” There may be no single correct state; it has to reason about symmetry, spacing, aesthetics, furniture placement, and household preferences.
“Put this somewhere safe.” “Safe” changes depending on whether the object is fragile, hot, valuable, dangerous to pets, sensitive to moisture, etc.
“Hide this somewhere the dog can’t reach it.” Requires reasoning about the pet’s reach, jumping ability, room access, and object safety.
“Move this out of the way.” It must infer where “out of the way” is without creating another obstruction.
“Fix this up.” The robot must determine what looks wrong before deciding what actions to take.
“Make this usable again.” Could mean clearing clutter, reconnecting something, cleaning it, reorganizing it, or finding missing components.
“Clear enough space for three people.” It must understand human body space, seating, walking clearance, and the activity being performed.
“Move the furniture around so we can watch the TV.” Requires understanding lines of sight and practical seating arrangements.
“Set this room back to normal.” Requires remembering the previous room state.
“You have ten minutes. Make this look better.” The robot must optimize its action sequence.
“Pack my bag for tomorrow.” Contents vary depending on destination and schedule.
“Pack for a weekend trip.” Requires selecting clothing and supplies based on duration, weather, planned activities, and available luggage space.
“Pack lightly.” The robot needs to optimize what is essential versus optional.
“Pack everything we might need.” The opposite objective, requiring uncertainty management.
“Unload the car and put everything away.” It has to classify items and route them to different locations.
“Bring in the groceries, but take the frozen stuff first.” Requires prioritizing temperature-sensitive items.
“Figure out where this new kitchen gadget should go.” Requires estimating frequency of use, size, compatibility with existing organization, and available space.
“Make more room in the refrigerator.” Requires rearranging containers while considering temperature zones, spills, expiration, and food safety.
“Take it off when it looks done.” “Done” is a perception and judgment problem.
“Cut these into roughly equal pieces.” Requires estimating volume, not simply following a predefined cut pattern.
“Cut this so everyone gets a fair piece.” Fairness may depend on size, toppings, preferences, or number of people.
“Use whichever pan makes sense.” The robot must select a tool from available options.
“Find something waterproof to put under this.” Requires material-property reasoning.
“Figure out how to open this.” The container may have a mechanism the robot has never encountered.
“Figure out how this latch works.” Requires visual and physical exploration.
“Open this without spilling it.” Manipulation must adapt to unknown contents and container geometry.
“Move this through that doorway.” Requires rotating and maneuvering bulky objects.
“Get this sofa around the corner.” A classic high-dimensional geometry and coordination problem.
“Move this upstairs.” Requires judging weight, balance, stair geometry, grip opportunities, and whether human assistance is necessary.
“Don’t move anything that looks intentional.” Requires interpreting arrangements rather than just object categories.
“Don’t disturb my setup.” It has to understand which relationships between objects must remain unchanged.
“Clean around this.” Requires preserving an existing configuration.
“Dust this shelf without knocking anything over.” Requires manipulating around dense, fragile clutter.
“Clean under there without moving everything.” Requires selecting tools and alternate approaches.
“Clean behind the couch.” The robot must determine whether it can reach, move the couch, use an attachment, or request help.
“Grab the thing next to the blue thing.” Requires resolving vague referring expressions.
“Give me that.” Requires gaze, pointing, conversation context, and object disambiguation.
“Put it over there.” Requires understanding gestures and shared spatial reference.
“Put it where I usually put it.” Requires personalized long-term memory.
“Make my room how it was yesterday.” Requires state reconstruction.
“Move this a little to the left.” Must resolve coordinate frame: robot-left, human-left, object's left, room-left, etc.
“Make the bed look hotel-quality.” Requires understanding a qualitative standard rather than just task completion.
“Fold this the way I normally fold it.” Personalized manipulation.
“Fold this weird-shaped thing.” Requires handling unseen deformable objects.
“Put this fitted sheet on the bed.” Deformable-object manipulation with corners that can be misidentified.
“Fold a fitted sheet.” Difficult even for many humans.
“Put this duvet into the cover.” Requires large deformable-object coordination.
“Figure out which corner goes where.” General correspondence reasoning.
“Close this drawer; something is blocking it.” Requires diagnosing the obstruction.
“The cabinet won’t close. Fix it.” It has to inspect contents and rearrange them.
“Find the matching sock.” Requires visual similarity under deformation and partial occlusion.
“Pair all these shoes.” Same challenge with orientation, size, color, and style.
“Put these clothes somewhere they won’t wrinkle.” Requires fabric/clothing knowledge.
“Hang whatever should be hung.” Requires garment classification.
“Move those chairs into the shade.” Shade changes spatially over time.
“Secure everything outside before the wind gets worse.” Requires deciding what can blow away, what needs folding, what needs moving, and what is already secure.
“Make a path through this clutter.” Requires choosing what can safely be moved and where.
“Clear a wheelchair path.” Requires understanding minimum practical clearance and accessibility.
“Make sure nobody trips over anything.” Requires hazard identification from a human perspective.
“Put fragile things somewhere safer before the kids come over.” Requires predicting future interactions.
“Follow me and carry these.” Combines tracking, navigation, load management, and obstacle avoidance.
“Hand me tools as I need them.” Requires predicting or recognizing stages in another person's work.
“Grab something that will work instead.” Requires tool substitution.
“Help me assemble this even though we lost the instructions.” Requires structural inference from parts.
“Figure out where this piece goes.” Requires matching geometry, function, and incomplete assemblies.
“Take this apart without breaking anything.” Requires discovering hidden fasteners and assembly sequence.
“Put this back together.” Requires remembering or inferring previous structure.
“Fix the wobbly table.” Requires diagnosing whether the issue is loose hardware, uneven floor, damaged leg, etc.
“Make this shelf level.” Requires sensing, adjustment, and iterative verification.
“Work around me.” Requires continuous path and manipulation replanning.
“Organize this however makes the most sense.” Requires generating its own organizational system.
“Reorganize this room now that we bought this new thing.” Requires adapting an existing organization system.
“Do this like I showed you last time.” Long-term skill memory.
“Keep the kids busy for ten minutes.” The robot must invent a safe, engaging game using only the objects currently available in the room.
“Arrange these flowers so they look nice.” Requires aesthetic planning, understanding balance, height, and color distribution.
“Stop.” / “Not like that.” / “Undo that.” Requires halting safely, working out what to revert, and restoring the prior state.
“Reach the top shelf.” Requires choosing a stool, reacher, or ladder, or asking for help.
“This lid’s stuck.” / “This window won’t open.” Requires loosening it without breaking it (heat, tapping, leverage, grip).
“Make Grandma comfortable.” Requires adapting temperature, seating, lighting, and reach to one specific person.
